biggest_risk: The planned spending in retirement would draw on the portfolio far faster than it could reasonably be expected to earn, so without changes the savings would shrink in real terms instead of lasting through a long retirement.
best_lever: With many years still ahead before retirement, raising the monthly contribution is the lever with the most room to work, because each added dollar saved now has the longest possible time to compound.
snapshot_intro: At this stage the plan does not yet reach the goal, and the grade reflects that gap honestly rather than softening it. The most useful fact here is also the most encouraging: almost everything that determines the outcome is still within reach, because retirement is many years away. This result reflects thousands of tested scenarios — including severe crashes and prolonged inflation — but cannot capture every possible risk such as legislative changes, major health issues, or divorce.
mirror_block: You are early in your working life with retirement still well ahead, which is the strongest asset in this whole file. Your savings sit across a registered retirement account, a tax-free account, and a small non-registered piece, and you add to them each month. In retirement your income would come from government benefits plus whatever the portfolio can support, since there is no workplace pension. The central tension is that the spending you have in mind would pull on the portfolio harder than it could grow, and that is the piece worth watching most closely.
revenue_analysis: The replacement level you are aiming for would keep your retirement lifestyle close in feel to your working years rather than asking you to scale down sharply. Because there is no workplace pension, the weight of sustaining that lifestyle would fall on the portfolio and on government benefits together. That structure can hold a continuous lifestyle, but only if the portfolio is built up enough over the years ahead to carry its share.
gov_explanation: Government benefits would form a dependable floor under your retirement income, one that arrives for life and does not depend on markets. That floor covers only a minority of your target spending, so the portfolio would need to carry the larger remainder. The years before benefits begin are a distinct bridge phase with little government support, which is a separate matter from the steady-state years once benefits are flowing.
longevity_analysis: The likely range of outcomes is wide, stretching from a cautious lower path where little or nothing remains to a more favorable upper path that still leaves a limited cushion. Half of all tested scenarios land somewhere inside that span, which tells you the result is sensitive to how the years actually unfold. You can hover over the projection to see how that range opens up at different ages.
priority_actions: What matters most for you is the distance between your planned spending and what the portfolio could realistically support, because that gap is what drives the whole result. At your intended pace, the savings would be drawn down quickly rather than stretching across a long retirement, which is the heart of the catch-up theme in your file. The next achievable step is not solving the entire gap at once but lifting the savings rate by a notch and holding it there — the long runway ahead would do much of the heavy lifting from there.
tax_analysis: Your tax rate today sits above where it would likely fall in retirement, which leaves room for registered contributions to work in your favour over time. The larger share of your savings is held in the registered retirement account, and that share would eventually face mandatory conversion to a Registered Retirement Income Fund in your early seventies. Planning the order of withdrawals well before that conversion could ease how heavily those later years are taxed.
estate_analysis: On the current path the projection shows nothing remaining as an estate in the typical case, and the cautious case is no different. That fits a plan where the savings are fully consumed to support spending rather than passed on. With your balanced preference, the focus would naturally fall on making the money last for you first, with any legacy as a later consideration once the plan is firmer.
obs_1: **Spending outpaces growth**: The pace at which your plan would draw on the portfolio runs far ahead of what that portfolio could be expected to earn in an average year, which means the savings would lose ground in real terms rather than gain it. This is the single relationship that turns a long runway into a tight outcome, and it is the one most worth correcting early.
obs_2: **Lifetime income floor**: Once Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security begin in your mid-sixties, the Guaranteed Income Supplement would join them to form a guaranteed monthly floor that covers a minority of your spending target. That floor lasts for life, but the years before it starts carry little government income, so the bridge phase and the steady-state phase ask very different things of your savings.
obs_3: **Rate drops in retirement**: Your effective tax rate would fall meaningfully once you stop earning a salary, freeing up income that is taxed lightly compared with today. That downward shift is exactly the gap that makes registered contributions now a sensible use of money that would otherwise be taxed at your higher working rate.
obs_4: **The long runway**: With many years still between you and retirement, a dollar saved today has the longest possible stretch to compound, and could grow several times over in real terms before you ever touch it. Time is the one input you have more of than almost anyone closer to retirement, and it works hardest on the dollars added earliest.
obs_5: **Discipline versus pace**: Your file shows steady saving habits but a spending plan that runs ahead of what those habits currently fund, so the friction is less about willingness to save and more about the size of the target. Narrowing that target or lifting the pace would close the gap from either direction, and you have the time for either to take hold.
next_horizon: The data suggests the years immediately ahead are the most valuable window you have, because contributions made now have the longest time to compound and the smallest change today carries the largest effect later. Acting while the runway is longest would matter more than any single later adjustment. The next update of this assessment, in a year, would measure how much an early change in pace has shifted the outcome.
model_blind_spots: The projection cannot see how you might draw down the registered account ahead of its mandatory conversion, which could change the tax picture in the later years. It also leaves out the life events most likely to reshape a plan at your stage — a career change, a raise, a move into a couple, or an inheritance — any of which could move the result sharply in either direction. These dimensions could be explored in a future review.
savings_analysis: The accumulation trajectory points upward over the years ahead, but its slope depends almost entirely on how much is added month to month rather than on what is already saved. The main driver is the contribution pace, since the starting balance is still a small part of what the plan would eventually need. The takeaway is that the years ahead, not the dollars already in place, decide where this ends up.
what_if_analysis: Among the scenarios tested, working longer moves the result more than any other single change, because it adds earning and saving years while shortening the stretch the money must cover. That sensitivity reveals a plan whose outcome hinges on time and contribution more than on market luck. It points to where the most reliable leverage sits for this profile.
strategy_comparison: Compared with staying on the status quo, working longer lifts the chance of success by the widest margin of the options modelled, while delaying Canada Pension Plan and saving more each offer smaller gains. Early Registered Retirement Savings Plan drawdown moves the other way, lowering the odds rather than helping. None of these alone closes the gap, which signals that more than one lever would likely need to move together.
fees_analysis: Your investment fees sit at a low level relative to typical products, so over the life of the plan they would quietly cost only a small fraction of your retirement income rather than a large one. That is a point in your favour and not the main story here. The interactive fee comparison lets you hover across several fee levels to see how much the gap between them would widen over time.
